body: Some milestones arrive one at a time, with a pause in the game and a ball handed to the equipment staff. Monday night in Minneapolis could deliver two of them in the same backfield, possibly in the same quarter. According to the Buffalo Bills' PR team, Josh Allen enters tonight's game at Minnesota (8:15 PM ET, ESPN/ABC) with 4,991 career rushing yards — nine yards short of 5,000. James Cook enters with 4,966 — thirty-four yards short of the exact same number, per the same Bills PR figures reported by Buffalowdown. A quarterback and his running back, crossing one of football's roundest numbers on the same night, in the same game, for the same team. Football almost never lines history up this neatly.

Start with Allen, because his version of 5,000 is the rarer one. If he gets his nine yards tonight — and against a Brian Flores defense that blitzes on roughly seven of every ten snaps, one scramble could do it — Allen will join Lamar Jackson, Michael Vick, Cam Newton and Russell Wilson as the only quarterbacks in NFL history with 5,000 career rushing yards, per Buffalowdown. That is the whole list. And Allen would arrive there in the middle of a season that is already bending record books: per NFL Research via the Vikings' official game preview, he is the first player in history with at least eight passing touchdowns (he has 11) and at least eight rushing touchdowns (he has nine) in his team's first seven games of a season. A week after he passed Jim Kelly's franchise touchdown-pass mark with Kelly in the building, Allen gets to join a five-man club that has no other active path in except Jackson. Nine yards. That is all that is standing between him and it.

Cook's 5,000 carries a different weight, because of where it would happen. Cook is the reigning NFL rushing champion, and he arrives in Minnesota with 707 rushing yards through seven games at 5.1 yards a carry and 101.0 rushing yards per game, per the Vikings' official preview — one of only three backs in football averaging over 100 a game. But U.S. Bank Stadium is not just another road dome for the Cook family. James is the younger brother of Dalvin Cook, who ran for four consecutive 1,000-yard seasons in this building for Minnesota from 2019 to 2022 after the Vikings drafted him to be Adrian Peterson's successor, per the same Vikings preview. And tonight, at halftime, Peterson himself will be inducted into the Vikings Ring of Honor as its 29th member, per DAZN's preview. The running back lineage of that stadium will be honored at halftime. The younger brother of the man who inherited it needs 34 yards to reach 5,000 of his own — in the other uniform, on the other sideline, in front of all of them.

The beautiful part for Buffalo is that chasing these numbers is not a distraction from the game plan — it IS the game plan. This site has spent all week on the central tension of tonight: Buffalo's No. 1 offense against Minnesota's No. 1 defense, and a Flores blitz machine that owns the league's best pressure and sack rates. The soft spot in that defense, all season, has been the ground. Minnesota is allowing 116 rushing yards per game, per ESPN figures cited by Buffalowdown, and 4.5 yards per carry — the number this site's Card desk flagged Saturday as the tax on Flores' aggression. Every Cook carry that stays ahead of the chains is a blitz that never gets called. Every Allen scramble that punishes a blitz is a defensive coordinator thinking twice about the next one. If Buffalo runs the ball the way it needs to run it to win this game, both milestones fall as a side effect of doing the right thing.

There is also a standings gift waiting if Buffalo finishes the job. Sunday was kind to the Bills without them taking a snap: all three other AFC East teams lost, per Buffalowdown, including New England's 45-27 loss to Green Bay in Foxborough, in which Drake Maye threw three interceptions as the Patriots committed four turnovers and never pulled within one score after the second quarter. The Patriots fell to 5-4. A Buffalo win tonight moves the Bills to 7-1, stretches the division lead, and turns New England's one win over Buffalo — that 29-26 Week 4 game — into an increasingly lonely argument. Milestones are the headline. Separation is the prize.

Two honest caveats before anyone engraves anything. First, the milestones are career regular-season rushing totals as the Bills' PR team counts them, and both men still have to actually gain the yards against the best defense in football — 34 yards for Cook is a good quarter's work most weeks, but this is not most weeks. Second, Buffalo's left side remains the game's biggest unknown: left tackle Dion Dawkins (rib) and left guard Alec Anderson (ankle) are both questionable after Dawkins missed the entire practice week, and tonight's inactives, about 90 minutes before kickoff, are the last word on who is blocking for the two men chasing history. If the backups start, the milestone watch gets harder and the survival watch gets louder — the same story this site has told since Thursday.

But sit with the shape of this night for a second, because Bills fans have earned the right to enjoy a setup like this. Six-and-one at six-and-one. The No. 1 offense against the No. 1 defense. A rematch of the 2022 classic. Peterson going into the Ring of Honor at halftime, a Cook in the visiting backfield 34 yards from 5,000, and a quarterback nine yards from a club that only four men have ever joined. History usually makes you wait. Tonight it has an appointment — 8:15 PM ET, in a loud dome, with two Bills racing each other to the same round number. Get there first, fellas. Go Bills — and get the full Monday night fallout in your inbox tomorrow morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: Saturday was supposed to bring an answer. Instead, Buffalo's final injury report for Monday night brought a tighter version of the same question. Left tackle Dion Dawkins did not practice on Saturday — his third straight missed practice with a rib injury — and the Bills listed him as questionable for Monday Night Football at Minnesota (Nov. 9, 8:15 PM ET, ESPN/ABC), per the final Week 9 report published by the Vikings and confirmed by Bills on SI. Three DNPs usually end the conversation. With Dawkins, Buffalo is deliberately not ending it.

The quotes explain why. Dawkins told reporters Friday, per Bills on SI: “I feel good. I've been winning my battles off of the field to try my best to be available on Monday.” Head coach Joe Brady backed that approach Saturday: “Some of these guys have played so much football, I have a trust that they know what their assignment is and that they can handle it,” Brady said, per the same report. “Had a conversation with Dion earlier in the week, and was like 'hey, let's do what we gotta do to be able to get to the game.' We'll continue to evaluate and play on Monday.” Translation: this is not a practice-reps decision. If Dawkins' ribs can take a hit Monday night, a man who has missed only two career starts due to injury, per Bills on SI, starts — zero practice week and all.

Dawkins is not the whole left side, and the other half moved the right way Saturday. Left guard Alec Anderson, who injured his ankle on the opening drive against Baltimore on Nov. 1, exited to the blue tent, returned after missing only two snaps and was later spotted in a walking boot leaving the locker room, per Bills on SI, was upgraded from did-not-practice to limited on Saturday and is also listed questionable, per the final report. Anderson getting any work in on the last day is a genuinely better sign than Dawkins' empty week — but questionable is questionable, and Buffalo could still be replacing one starter, or two, on Josh Allen's blind side. If Dawkins cannot go, backup Tylan Grable will prepare to replace him at left tackle, per Bills on SI.

Now the good column, because Saturday delivered plenty of it and it should not get buried under the headline. Right tackle Spencer Brown improved to a full participant Saturday and carries no game designation — he has been cleared for Monday night after missing the Baltimore game with a back injury, per Bills on SI and the final report. The red-jersey crew is cleared too: wide receiver DJ Moore (shoulder), tight end Dalton Kincaid (chest) and wide receiver Keon Coleman (shoulder) all carry no designation and have been cleared for Week 9, per Bills on SI. Cornerback Dee Alford was a full participant all week, Khalil Shakir returned Saturday after Friday's personal absence, and running back Ty Johnson is back to full, per the final report. The offense Allen will actually throw to is intact. The question is only who is standing in front of it.

The rest of Buffalo's designations are narrower. Wide receiver Joshua Palmer (hamstring) is out — the only Bill ruled out — after missing practice all week, per the final report. Defensive tackle Greg Gaines (calf) was upgraded to limited Saturday and is questionable. Defensive back Jordan Hancock (hamstring) and wide receiver Tyrell Shavers (knee) are also questionable, and both would need to be activated — Hancock from injured reserve, Shavers from the physically unable to perform list — to play Monday, per NBC Sports. Those are roster-move questions for Monday afternoon, not just injury questions.

Minnesota's final report, for its part, mostly closed doors Buffalo already knew about. Quarterback Kyler Murray (hamstring), running back Demond Claiborne (knee) and receiver Jauan Jennings (calf) are out, and safeties Theo Jackson (quad) and Jay Ward (knee) are questionable, per the Vikings' final report. Tackle Christian Darrisaw, linebacker Jake Golday, cornerback Isaiah Rodgers and outside linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel received no designations and are expected to be available, per the same report. Carson Wentz starts at quarterback — settled since Thursday — which means the Vikings' defense, not their offense, remains the fully loaded half of this matchup.

And that is why a rib injury in Orchard Park is the biggest story of a Sunday the Bills do not even play on. Minnesota records a sack on 12.32 percent of all pass attempts and gets home more frequently than any other unit in the NFL, per Bills on SI — the pass rush Buffalo's patched left side would meet in the loudest building on the schedule. A whole offensive line makes Monday night what it was billed as all week: the league's No. 1 offense against its No. 1 defense, 6-1 against 6-1. A backup left side makes it something else entirely — a survival test Allen has passed before, but never one Joe Brady would volunteer for.

So Sunday in Buffalo is a waiting room. Bills fans get the afternoon slate — including New England, the only team to beat Buffalo this season, hosting Green Bay at 4:25 PM ET, per Athlon — and then one more day of not knowing. Questionable is not a verdict, and this desk will not print it as one: Monday's inactives, about 90 minutes before kickoff, are the last word on Dawkins, Anderson, Gaines and the activation calls. Until then, the most honest sentence in football is the one on Buffalo's final report: Dion Dawkins, rib, did not practice, questionable. Everything about Monday night runs through whether that changes by game time. Go Bills — and get the inactives and the full Monday night fallout in your inbox every morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: Welcome back to The Card — I'm Matt Manzella, and this is the one desk on this site where we talk about the numbers that move money. This is Partner Content, presented by Kalshi, the regulated exchange where you trade on game outcomes instead of betting against a house. The rule here has not changed since this desk opened: every number below traces to a named source, every position gets logged in public, and there are no locks and no guarantees. Anyone selling you certainty on a Monday night game in November is selling you a feeling. The Card sells homework — and this week's homework changed on Friday afternoon.

Start with the headline price. Buffalo (6-1) visits Minnesota (6-1) on Monday night, Nov. 9 at 8:15 PM ET on ESPN at U.S. Bank Stadium, and the Associated Press preview has the Bills as a 3.5-point road favorite. On paper, that price is easy to defend: per the same AP preview, Buffalo has scored 30 or more points in three straight games and five of seven, and James Cook arrives with 707 rushing yards, fifth in the league. The market is pricing the No. 1 offense in football. What the market cannot fully price yet — because the Bills themselves do not know it yet — is who is blocking for that offense.

Here is what Friday did to the left side of Buffalo's line. Per Buffalo Rumblings' Friday injury report, left tackle Dion Dawkins missed a second straight practice with the rib injury he says he suffered in the first quarter of last Sunday's win over Baltimore; Dawkins told reporters he plans to be ready to go Monday night, but a plan is not a practice rep. Left guard Alec Anderson also missed a second straight day with an ankle injury after being seen in a boot following the Ravens game, and Rumblings' assessment was blunt: Anderson likely misses Monday, leaving Tylan Grable or Austin Corbett to fill the spot. Right tackle Spencer Brown, who missed the Baltimore game with a back injury, was limited for a second straight day; Rumblings expects a questionable tag when final designations land Saturday, with an expectation he suits up — an expectation, not a designation, and this desk will not trade it as one. Three starters, three question marks, forty-eight hours before Brian Flores.

And Flores is the worst possible opponent for a patched line, because his defense is not a pass rusher — it is a weather system. Per the Democrat and Chronicle's Saturday matchup breakdown, Minnesota owns the NFL's No. 1 scoring defense at 13.3 points allowed per game; its 93 points allowed through seven games are the franchise's fewest at this point since 1986, and its 10 fourth-quarter points allowed are the fewest in the league through seven games since the 2019 Patriots allowed seven. The Vikings blitz on 71% of plays, per the same breakdown — the next closest team, Carolina, sits at 42.6% — and in the last two weeks Flores blitzed Indianapolis' Daniel Jones on 85.2% of his dropbacks and Detroit's Jared Goff on 79.3%, per Sumer Sports charting cited by the Democrat and Chronicle. Minnesota ranks No. 1 in both sack percentage (10.5%) and pressure rate (45.8%). That is the defense a backup left side would be walking into, in the loudest dome in football.

Now the other side of the ledger, because The Card does not do one-sided math. Josh Allen has been blitzed on 33.2% of his dropbacks this season and has made teams pay for it, per the Democrat and Chronicle: 66.7% completions at 8.6 yards per attempt with three touchdowns against the blitz, plus 204 scramble yards — fourth-most in the league — including a league-best 11 quarterback runs of 10 or more yards. A blitz that misses Allen does not just fail; it donates a first down. And Cook is the pressure release the whole plan runs through: per Buffalo Rumblings' five Bills to watch, the one soft number on Minnesota's defensive sheet is 4.5 yards allowed per carry. Every efficient Cook run is a Flores blitz that never gets called and a third-and-manageable instead of a third-and-9 in a shaking dome. Friday also brought Buffalo one genuine piece of good news the headline price may not have caught: tight end Dalton Kincaid was upgraded to a full participant, per Rumblings, after a week limited by a chest injury. Khalil Shakir's Friday absence was personal, not medical, per the same report. And Minnesota's own report moved the wrong way in the backfield — running back Demond Claiborne was downgraded to did-not-practice with a knee injury — even as the Vikings got left tackle Christian Darrisaw and cornerback Isaiah Rodgers back to full practice, per Rumblings and the Daily Norseman.

The Minnesota quarterback situation, at least, is settled, and it matters to the total picture: Carson Wentz starts Monday night with Kyler Murray out with a hamstring strain and considered week-to-week, per Reuters. Wentz is a pocket passer without Murray's escape hatch, facing a Buffalo defense that just played its best game of the season — but a veteran pocket passer feeding Justin Jefferson on time is exactly how a frustrated superstar stops slumping, and this site's Culture Desk already told that story this week. Price the quarterback who is actually playing: a stationary target for Jim Leonhard's blitz, and a live risk to Christian Benford on the other end of it.

So here is my card for Monday night, in order. One: the Cook angle — Buffalo's run game is the tax on Flores' blitz rate, and 4.5 yards a carry allowed is the number I trust most on either sheet; if Buffalo controls this game, it controls it on the ground first. Two: patience on the game itself until Saturday's final designations — if Dawkins is cleared and Brown carries only a questionable tag, Buffalo's price makes sense; if Dawkins is out and the left side is two backups deep, the honest position is no position until the live market overreacts to Minnesota's first blitz that gets home. Three: Buffalo to win is still my lean — Allen's anti-blitz numbers are real, and this offense has hit 30 in three straight — but it is a lean that lives and dies with the Saturday report, and I will check the live price on Kalshi before trading anything, because the number moves with every injury headline out of Orchard Park.

Prices move, nothing in this column is a guarantee, and this is analysis and entertainment, not financial advice. Trade only what you can afford to lose. body: Thursday was supposed to simplify Monday night. It did — for Minnesota. Vikings head coach Kevin O'Connell announced Thursday that Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring strain and Carson Wentz will start against Buffalo at U.S. Bank Stadium (Monday, 8:15 PM ET, ESPN), with Max Brosmer backing him up. One sideline got its answer three days early. The other sideline opened its first practice report of the week and found a different kind of problem: 18 players listed, per Bills on SI's count — and the top of the list is Buffalo's offensive line, three days before it meets the No. 1 defense in football.

Start with the quarterback change, because it is real news and not a smokescreen. Per Reuters, Murray is considered week-to-week after imaging confirmed the hamstring strain he suffered late in Sunday's 19-15 loss in Detroit, and O'Connell said the team does not expect him to land on injured reserve. In his place: Wentz, 33, making his 101st career start and his second of this season. His 2026 line in two appearances, per Reuters, is 23 of 39 for 276 yards with three touchdowns and no interceptions — he relieved Murray in the Sept. 13 opener and helped beat Green Bay 39-22, then started the 9-3 win at Chicago the following week. Minnesota is apparently not done shopping, either: per James Palmer of NFL on Prime, the Vikings have been working the phones about quarterback depth ahead of Tuesday's trade deadline and have not ruled out adding to the room. None of that changes Monday. Monday is Wentz.

For Jim Leonhard, that changes the test — it does not erase it. Murray's threat was his legs and the chaos that follows them; Wentz is a pocket passer who, per Athlon's breakdown, was sacked six times in his limited duty this season and does not have Murray's escape hatch. If the aggressive, booth-called defense Buffalo unveiled against Baltimore — 61.3% blitz, season-high man coverage, per Buffalo Rumblings' charting — was ever going to get a second audition, a stationary target in prime time is the invitation. But do not write Wentz off as a relief pitcher. He has thrown for 23,902 yards and 162 touchdowns across 100 career starts, per Reuters, he is 2-0 in the games he has played this season, and there is one uncomfortable fit for Buffalo: the thing Minnesota's offense has failed to do for two months is get Justin Jefferson the ball accurately — Athlon counted four inaccurate Murray overthrows on Jefferson's nine targets in Detroit — and a veteran pocket passer feeding his best receiver on time is exactly how a 'frustrated superstar' story, the one this site's Culture Desk told yesterday, stops being a slump. Christian Benford's rematch with Jefferson just got a different quarterback throwing the ball.

Now the part of Thursday that should actually worry Bills fans, because it is Buffalo's. Per the Bills' first official report of the week, reported by NBC Sports and the Democrat and Chronicle: left tackle Dion Dawkins did not practice with a rib injury — a new name, and Josh Allen's blind-side protector. Left guard Alec Anderson did not practice with an ankle injury; Bills reporter Jon Scott noted Anderson was wearing a boot after Sunday's game, per Heavy. And right tackle Spencer Brown was limited with the back injury that already cost him the Ravens game, when Tylan Grable started in his place, per Bills on SI. That is both starting tackles and a starting guard on the same report, in the same week, against Brian Flores — whose defense, as this site's Film Room detailed Wednesday, has blitzed at a 69.9% rate this season, per TSN, a number no team has approached since ESPN Research began tracking pass rushes in 2006. Buffalo's offense is the story of this season. Thursday, its foundation was the injury report.

The rest of the report cuts both ways, and the honest version includes the good column. Did not practice: wide receiver Joshua Palmer (hamstring — Bills on SI reports he is expected to miss multiple weeks), defensive tackle Greg Gaines (calf) and running back Ty Johnson (illness, which Buffalo Rumblings expects to clear quickly). Limited: Brown, DJ Moore (shoulder), Keon Coleman (shoulder), Dalton Kincaid (chest) and defensive back Jordan Hancock (hamstring, in his return-from-IR window), per NBC Sports. Full practice — and this matters — slot corner Dee Alford, back at full strength after missing two weeks, per Buffalo Rumblings, plus Ed Oliver, Bradley Chubb, TJ Parker, Ar'maj Reed-Adams and T.J. Sanders. And Tyrell Shavers practiced fully in his PUP window; Buffalo has until Nov. 19 to activate him, per Rumblings. A Thursday report for a Monday game is a weather vane, not a verdict: final game designations arrive Saturday, and Monday's inactives, about 90 minutes before kickoff, are the last word. This desk will not print a practice report as a lineup.

But understand what rides on Friday's and Saturday's updates, because the stakes are not abstract. Per the Associated Press preview carried by TSN, Buffalo has hit 30 points in three straight games and five of seven, has scored on 43 of its 70 drives that did not end in a kneel-down, and Monday is the first time since 2013 that a team averaging 33 or more points has played a team allowing 14 or fewer this late in a season. James Cook enters with 707 rushing yards, fifth in the league, per the same preview — and every one of those numbers runs behind the five men Thursday's report just put in question. Buffalo is a 3.5-point road favorite, per the AP's need-to-know, and that price assumes something close to a whole offensive line. If Dawkins returns to practice Friday and Brown stacks a second limited day, this becomes a footnote. If the DNP column holds, Monday night stops being No. 1 offense versus No. 1 defense and becomes a survival drill — Allen improvising behind backups against the most aggressive defense in football.

So the weekend watch is simple, and it is not in Minneapolis. It is the left side of Buffalo's practice report. Minnesota answered its biggest question on Thursday; Buffalo's biggest question — who protects Josh Allen on Monday night — does not get answered until the weekend, and Flores gets a vote either way. Go Bills — and get every injury update and the full Monday night fallout in your inbox every morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: There is a catch Buffalo fans can still see with their eyes closed. Fourth-and-18. Two minutes left. Minnesota trailing 27-23 at the old Highmark Stadium in November 2022, the game basically over — until Kirk Cousins threw a prayer toward the sideline and Justin Jefferson went up over Cam Lewis, got one hand on a ball Lewis had two hands on, wrestled it away as they fell, and kept it off the turf for 32 yards. Per the Democrat and Chronicle's rematch look published Thursday, that was arguably the catch of that NFL season, maybe the best catch of Jefferson's career. On Monday night at U.S. Bank Stadium — 6-1 Buffalo at 6-1 Minnesota, 8:15 PM ET — Jefferson gets his second-ever game against the Bills. The first one still haunts this fan base. That is not a metaphor. It is the preview.

Run the whole 2022 afternoon back, because Monday only means what it means against that memory. Jefferson was targeted 16 times by Cousins that day and caught 10 for 193 yards and a touchdown, per the Democrat and Chronicle — in the season he finished as the NFL's Offensive Player of the Year. After the fourth-and-18 miracle, he appeared to catch the go-ahead touchdown, only for replay to rule him just short; Buffalo stopped Cousins on a sneak and thought it had survived. Then Josh Allen fumbled, Eric Kendricks recovered in the end zone, Tyler Bass tied it with two seconds left anyway, and Allen's overtime interception to Patrick Peterson at the Minnesota 20 ended a 33-30 Vikings win. Minnesota finished with 481 yards, Cousins threw for 357, and Dalvin Cook — James Cook's older brother — ran for 119, including the 81-yard touchdown that started the rally from 27-10 down. Buffalo has faced the two-time All-Pro Jefferson exactly once, per the Democrat and Chronicle. Once was plenty.

So here is the twist nobody in Buffalo saw coming four years ago: the Jefferson walking into this rematch is not destroying anybody right now — and he knows it. For the season, per the Democrat and Chronicle, Jefferson has 28 catches on 40 targets for 335 yards and four touchdowns, with no eruption to point to, on a Minnesota offense that ranks 27th in scoring at 20.0 points per game, 29th in yards at 279.4 and 31st in passing yards at 165.6. Last Sunday in Detroit was supposed to be the get-right game against a struggling defense. Instead the Lions held Minnesota to 15 points and 266 yards in the Vikings' first loss, Jefferson caught five passes for 33 yards — one of them, to be fair, a tremendous one-handed touchdown — and afterward, per the same reporting, the normally affable Jefferson blew off reporters in the locker room. Athlon's Week 9 breakdown counted four inaccurate overthrows on his nine targets in that game. The best receiver in football is open, frustrated, and watching his quarterback miss him.

His quarterback is not hiding from it. “Obviously he's frustrated, and that's understandable,” Kyler Murray said, per the Democrat and Chronicle. “He is who he is, and he has every right to the way he feels when he doesn't get the ball. That's on us to find a way to get him the ball.” Head coach Kevin O'Connell, asked Monday whether Jefferson's irritation is showing, called him “the ultra-competitor” who sets the standard, and pointed to the double-team attention Jefferson draws on known passing downs — attention that, in O'Connell's telling, means somebody else has to make a play. The numbers underneath are colder: per the Democrat and Chronicle, Murray's passing success rate sits at 38.5%, 26th among starters, against Allen's 50%, sixth. And Minnesota is monitoring Murray's hamstring this week, per the Bills' own Week 9 storylines — Bills.com noted the soreness cropped up in the fourth quarter against Detroit and that Murray needed treatment Monday. That is a storyline to track into Saturday's game-status report for a Monday game, not a designation to assume in either direction.

Which is exactly what makes Monday dangerous in the specific way Bills fans recognize in their stomachs. A superstar's slump does not lower his ceiling; it loads it. Buffalo's side of the matchup has a name, too: per Bills on SI's Week 9 look at the Bills with the most to prove, published Thursday via Yardbarker, Christian Benford will find himself lined up across from Jefferson for much of the game — the matchup that site called one of the best to watch all weekend, against a route-running wizard who is unguardable when he is on top of his game and who can light up a scoreboard without warning. Benford was a rookie in that 2022 game. He is Buffalo's top corner now. There is no hiding him from this assignment, and, honestly, there should not be: this is the rematch inside the rematch.

Defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard, at least publicly, is refusing to buy the slump. “We play a team that's 6-1,” Leonhard said, per the Democrat and Chronicle. “What doesn't necessarily matter — offensively, defensively — is how they're getting it done and they know how to win, right? And that's the trick of the NFL is do you know how to win. We're gonna go to Minnesota and play a team that knows how to do that right now.” That respect is earned context, not coach-speak filler: Leonhard's defense just played its best game of the season against Baltimore, all of it — as this site's Film Room laid out Tuesday — carrying the asterisk of Lamar Jackson's first-snap thumb injury and a third-string rookie finishing the game. Jefferson, even a starving Jefferson, attached to a starting quarterback, is a different kind of test than a backup's backup. If Buffalo's suddenly aggressive booth-called defense holds Jefferson to another 33-yard night, the asterisk conversation ends. If Jefferson finally erupts, it will not be a surprise to anyone who remembers 2022. It will feel like a sequel.

That is why, in a week this site has already spent on the No. 1 offense meeting the No. 1 defense, the Culture Desk keeps coming back to one man in a purple helmet. Games like Monday's get remembered for a single play — Buffalo fans of all people know that; we have been remembering one for four years, against our will, in high definition. Jefferson does not need 193 yards to change Monday night. He needs one fourth-quarter moment where the ball is in the air, a Bills defender is in perfect position, and the whole stadium understands at the same time that perfect position was not enough the last time. Benford and Leonhard's defense get to write the ending this time. Make Jefferson's quiet season stay quiet for one more week, and Buffalo leaves Minneapolis 7-1 with the ghost finally buried. Let him wake up, and Bills Mafia will have a second catch to see in its sleep. Go Bills — and get the full Monday night fallout in your inbox every morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: Monday night in Minneapolis is not just 6-1 against 6-1. It is the rarest kind of regular-season collision the modern NFL produces. When Buffalo visits the Minnesota Vikings on Monday, Nov. 9 at 8:15 PM ET at U.S. Bank Stadium, it will be just the seventh time since 2017 that the No. 1 offense in EPA per play meets the No. 1 defense in EPA allowed per play, per Buffalo Rumblings' breakdown published Wednesday. EPA per play is not a vanity ranking — Rumblings notes it is a truer measure of a unit's quality than yards or points alone. So strip away the records, the dome and the prime-time lights, and Monday is simple: the best offense in football, against the best defense in football, with one of them walking out looking ordinary.

History says 'ordinary' is exactly what happens — to somebody. The previous six No. 1-versus-No. 1 meetings split evenly, 3-3, per Rumblings: the Ravens beat the Patriots in 2019, the Buccaneers humbled Green Bay in 2020, Buffalo itself beat Kansas City in 2021, Tampa Bay beat Buffalo in overtime later that season, the Chiefs rolled the 49ers in 2022, and the Texans edged the Colts last season. Stretch the sample back to 2001 and the No. 1 offense holds a modest 10-6 edge — but the cost of the ticket shows up in the numbers. The No. 1 offense in those games averaged just 25.6 points, its EPA per play collapsed from +0.217 entering the game to +0.059 during it, and in seven of the 16 matchups the best offense in football actually posted a negative EPA per play. Nobody stays No. 1 on both sides of the ball Monday night. Somebody's ranking is a costume, and the game strips it off.

The defense trying to do the stripping belongs to Brian Flores, and it does not bluff so much as it floods. Minnesota has blitzed at a 69.9% rate this season, per TSN's tracking — a figure no team has approached through seven weeks since ESPN Research began tracking pass rushes in 2006, against a league historical average of 28.9%. Against Indianapolis, Flores sent extra rushers on 85.2% of Daniel Jones' dropbacks, the highest single-game blitz rate of the Next Gen Stats era. And yet the twist that should worry Joe Brady most is the opposite one: per the same TSN reporting, Minnesota's defensive EPA has been substantially better when it rushes four or fewer than when it blitzes. The threat of the blitz is the weapon. Flores, who praised Josh Allen's development at length this week, per ClutchPoints, does not need to send six to beat you — he needs you to spend all week preparing for six, then beat you with four and a coverage picture that changed after the snap.

That coverage picture is the second half of the chess match. Per NBC Sports' matchup breakdown, Minnesota plays the fewest man coverage in the NFL at 5.3% and the second-most zone at 86.5% — a defense that keeps its eyes on the quarterback, rallies to the ball and dares Allen to be patient for twelve plays at a time. Allen, per the same breakdown, has completed 69.7% of his passes against zone this season, and he arrives with the season line ClutchPoints cited this week: 135 of 205 for 1,793 yards, 11 touchdowns and five interceptions, fresh off a three-total-touchdown afternoon against Baltimore in which he threw for 289 yards. Patience, though, has never been the question with Allen. The question is whether patience survives the fourth quarter of a one-score game in a dome that is shaking — because that is exactly when No. 17 stops dinking, starts hunting, and gives a zone defense the one thing it is built to steal.

Which is why James Cook might be the most important Bill in Minneapolis. Minnesota's defense finally cracked last week, losing its first game of the season, 19-15 in Detroit — and per Vikings Territory's Week 9 breakdown, the Lions torched the Vikings on the ground in that loss. Cook is the reigning NFL rushing champion, and his 2026 log, per Pro Football Network, reads 138 carries for 707 yards at 5.1 a carry with seven touchdowns through seven games. Every efficient Cook run is a blitz that never gets called, a third-and-manageable instead of a third-and-9 against a defense that lives for obvious passing downs, and a minute of rest for Buffalo's own defense. If Buffalo has to drop back 45 times to win this game, Flores wins the math even if he loses some snaps. If Cook forces Minnesota to defend the run honestly, Allen gets to play against a defense that is guessing — and nobody in football guesses worse for Flores than a quarterback who can also run through the blitz when it finally does come.

The honest caveats belong on the record before kickoff. Minnesota's offense is the weak half of its own building — it has struggled all season behind a defense carrying the record — and quarterback Kyler Murray is questionable with a hamstring injury but expected to play, per NBC Sports. For Buffalo, the week's real information has not arrived yet: a Monday game means the Bills' first practice report does not land until Thursday, and the names to watch on it are wide receivers Joshua Palmer, who injured his hamstring against Baltimore, and DJ Moore, who gave Buffalo a late knee scare Sunday before saying afterward that he was OK, per NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe — plus right tackle Spencer Brown, who missed the Ravens game with a back issue. None of those are designations, and Film Room will not print them as such. They are the difference between Buffalo arriving at full strength for a No. 1-versus-No. 1 fight and arriving with duct tape on the edges.

So here is the verdict history hands us, and it is the only prediction this matchup honestly supports. Buffalo's offense will not look like the No. 1 offense in football for four quarters Monday night — nobody's does in these games; the EPA cliff from +0.217 to +0.059 is the tax the No. 1 defense collects. The game will be won in the margins the rankings do not capture: whether Cook keeps Flores honest, whether Allen takes the zone's underneath money without forcing the deep shot that ends a drive, and whether Jim Leonhard's suddenly aggressive Buffalo defense — the story of last Sunday — can hold a struggling Minnesota offense to the kind of night where 24 points is enough. The No. 1 offense scores 25.6 points on average in these games, per Rumblings. In a dome, in prime time, against this blitz, 25 points and a defense that just found itself might be exactly the formula. One ranking falls Monday night. Film Room is betting it is not Buffalo's. Go Bills — and get the full Monday night breakdown in your inbox every morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: The Buffalo Bills announced Tuesday that they are releasing safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson — one day after his one-game suspension ended, and six days before the biggest game of their season. Gardner-Johnson became eligible to return to the roster on Monday. Instead of a return, he got a release.

It is a stunning end to a short stay. Buffalo signed Gardner-Johnson to a one-year deal in March, and he started all six games he played alongside Cole Bishop, finishing with 26 tackles, two passes defended and one interception. Two weeks ago, head coach Joe Brady stood in front of reporters and defended him — "C.J.'s a member of the Buffalo Bills. We brought him here for a reason." On Tuesday, the Bills decided the reason had run out.

The unraveling started in the Week 6 win over the Raiders, when Gardner-Johnson was ejected before halftime for spitting toward tight end Brock Bowers. The NFL suspended him one game without pay. He appealed, the suspension was upheld, and he sat out Sunday's 36-10 win over Baltimore — a week that also brought an additional $11,194 fine for unnecessary roughness in the Raiders game.

If you are assuming the spitting got him cut, the reporting says otherwise. Per NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe, the release was driven by Gardner-Johnson's inconsistency in play — too many snaps that left the staff wondering what he was doing. The numbers back it up: after two strong outings to open the season, quarterbacks posted passer ratings of 92.4, 126.6 and 118.7 throwing his way in the three weeks before the bye, per figures cited by Sporting News. The edge he brought was real. So was the volatility.

And then there is the timing Buffalo cannot ignore: this defense just played its best game of the season without him. Against Baltimore, the Bills allowed 144 total yards, held Derrick Henry to 53 rushing yards, kept Zay Flowers without a single catch and forced three turnovers — with Damar Hamlin stepping back into the lineup and Te'Cory Couch earning praise from Brady after the game. The front office watched that film and chose the room it had over the name it signed.

Couch, signed to the active roster on Oct. 31 with the roster spot the suspension opened, keeps his place on the 53. Hamlin is in line to start next to Bishop on Monday night, with Sam Franklin Jr. and rookie Jalon Kilgore behind them and Geno Stone on the practice squad. The first test could not be much bigger: Monday Night Football in Minnesota, 6-1 against 6-1.

Gardner-Johnson is 28, a Super Bowl champion, and now heads to waivers looking for his eighth stop — a career that has never lacked for talent or headlines. Somebody will call; starting-caliber safeties are scarce in November. But Buffalo, holding the AFC's best record, just told you what it values more: eleven guys playing the same defense over one guy playing his own. Was it the right call? Tell us below — and get the full breakdown in your inbox every morning with The BNC Blitz.

body: For six games, Jim Leonhard's defense had a calling card, and it was not a flattering one: heavy personnel, heavy boxes, the most Cover 4 in the league, a narrow menu of coverages, very little press and very little blitzing — a profile Buffalo Rumblings laid out in its look at this defense two weeks ago, attached to rankings of 30th in EPA per play allowed and 28th in success rate against. Then Baltimore came to town on Sunday, and Leonhard called a different sport. In Rumblings' tendency breakdown published Tuesday, Bruce Nolan charted season highs across the board in the 36-10 win: man coverage on 54.8% of snaps, a 61.3% blitz rate, middle-of-the-field-closed coverages on 67.7%, and pre-snap two-high looks rotating down to one-high after the snap at a season-high 25.8% rate. Press coverage, already rare, vanished entirely — 0.0%, down from a previous season low of 7.9%. And Leonhard called all of it from a new address: the booth, a move he said helped smooth out the operation, per Rumblings.

One of those changes is already confirmed as permanent — or as close to permanent as anything gets in November. Per Rumblings, head coach Joe Brady said at his Monday press conference that Leonhard's presence in the booth is the one change from Sunday that is definitively likely to continue. That matters more than it sounds. A coordinator in the booth sees route combinations and substitutions the way a quarterback in the film room does, a beat earlier and a layer cleaner, and if the price of that vision is losing the sideline huddle, Brady has clearly decided the trade is worth it. The blitz-and-man package that came with the booth debut, though? That is where Film Room has to slow everybody down — starting with the asterisk that swallowed Baltimore's whole afternoon.

The asterisk has a name and a thumb. Lamar Jackson injured the thumb on his throwing hand on Baltimore's first offensive snap, when his hand struck Greg Rousseau, and was replaced by Tyler Huntley, who himself later left with a toe injury, leaving undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano to finish his NFL debut. Rumblings is blunt about what that does to the data: every tendency change has to be heavily couched through the lens of Jackson's injury. Would Buffalo have blitzed 61% of the time with one of the greatest rushing quarterbacks ever standing across the line, free to punish a blitz that missed? Would it have played that much man coverage — defenders turning their backs to the quarterback — if the quarterback was Jackson instead of a third-string rookie? Nobody in Orchard Park can honestly answer yes, and the film cannot answer it for them.

What the film can say is what the plan did to the game in front of it. Baltimore finished with 144 total yards, three turnovers, four sacks taken and 12 quarterback hits absorbed, per Buffalowdown's recap of the win — and the tendency numbers explain the texture of that beating. Man coverage with a closed middle is a bet that your rush gets home before a receiver separates, and a 61.3% blitz rate is how you make sure the bet cashes: the quarterback holds the ball against tight coverage, the extra rusher arrives, and the throw that does come out is hurried into a defense that has already rotated into its one-high picture. The result nudged Buffalo's season rankings up to 24th in both points allowed (25.9 per game) and yards allowed (352.1), per the Democrat and Chronicle — still not a good defense on paper, but no longer the league's basement address it carried into the bye at 28.5 points allowed per game.

The personnel underneath the plan quietly cooperated, too. Ed Oliver, back after missing two games with a knee injury, played 20 snaps and registered three quarterback hits without a tackle, per the Democrat and Chronicle's injury update — exactly the kind of interior disruption a blitz-heavy plan needs, because the extra rusher only stays extra if the front four wins its share alone. TJ Parker, active after a questionable tag, added two tackles and a sack. And the back end gets a name back this week: safety C.J. Gardner-Johnson, whose one-game suspension was upheld on appeal, served his game against Baltimore and became eligible to return to the active roster on Nov. 2. Man coverage is a coverage you call with your best cover players available. Last Sunday, Buffalo called it without one of them.

Which brings us to the only test that counts. Buffalo (6-1) visits Minnesota (6-1) on Monday Night Football, Nov. 9 at 8:15 PM ET at U.S. Bank Stadium — and the Vikings' offense is, on paper, the mirror image of their blitzing, league-leading defense: Minnesota ranks 27th in scoring at 20.0 points per game and 29th in yards at 279.4, per the Democrat and Chronicle's matchup breakdown. If there was ever a week to find out whether Sunday's aggression was an identity or an accident of circumstance, it is against an offense that has struggled to punish anybody — with the honest Week 9 questions attached: early-week reporting listed Vikings quarterback Kyler Murray managing hamstring tightness, and Buffalo's first participation report for a Monday game does not arrive until Thursday, so the Sunday exits of Joshua Palmer (hamstring) and DJ Moore (knee), plus Spencer Brown, Greg Gaines and Dee Alford missing the Ravens game, are storylines to track this week, not designations to assume.

So here is the Film Room verdict, and it is deliberately two sentences long. The booth is real — Brady said so on Monday, and it stays. Everything else — the 61% blitz, the 55% man, the zero press, the disguised rotations — gets its verdict under the Monday night lights in Minneapolis, against a starting quarterback, in a 6-1-versus-6-1 game Buffalo cannot afford to treat as a laboratory. If Leonhard dials it up again and it works, Sunday was not a mirage produced by an injured thumb; it was the day this defense found itself. If the Cover 4 comes back, we will know Sunday was a one-week costume. Either way, for the first time all season, the most interesting unit on this team might not be the one with Josh Allen on it. Go Bills.

Brady confirmed the booth stays. Monday night in Minnesota decides whether the rest was real.

body: Some records fall in empty stadiums in December, in games nobody will remember, and get a polite line in the game notes. Josh Allen's fell the other way. With 12:18 left in the fourth quarter on Sunday at Highmark Stadium, Allen hit DJ Moore for an 11-yard touchdown on third-and-8 — and that throw, per Reuters and the Bills' own recap, was the 259th touchdown pass of Allen's career, regular season and playoffs combined. One more than Jim Kelly. And Kelly was in the building to watch it happen, as Buffalo closed out a 36-10 win over the Baltimore Ravens to move to 6-1.

Get the math straight, because this desk respects the man whose record it was. Kelly's 258 was built the hard way: 237 regular-season touchdowns and 21 more in the playoffs, per Reuters. Allen entered Sunday tied with him at 258, per Buffalo Rumblings, and the Moore touchdown — his 230th regular-season scoring throw, per Reuters — put him alone on top of the combined list. He was not done: a 23-yard touchdown to Dalton Kincaid with 5:58 left made it 260 combined. One honest asterisk, offered proudly rather than hidden: Kelly still owns the regular-season-only record, 237 to Allen's 231. That countdown is now six throws long, and it is the next piece of history on the schedule.

The record also arrived the way Allen's career usually does — not in a clean game, but in a woken-up one. Buffalo led just 16-10 early in the third quarter after a mistake-filled first half, and then Allen took the game over. Per the Bills' official recap, he completed 13 of 15 passes for 177 yards and two touchdowns after halftime, a 155.4 passer rating, as Buffalo outscored Baltimore 20-3 in the second half. His final line: 21 of 34 for 289 yards, two passing touchdowns and one interception, plus the 1-yard rushing touchdown that opened the scoring. Allen did it, per the same reporting, in his 150th career game — Kelly's 258 came across 177 games. Different eras, different offenses, one record book, and the new name got there faster.

The two men who caught the record throws deserve their lines, because both were question marks on Friday. Moore, back after missing two games with a shoulder injury, finished with four catches for 82 yards and the record-setting touchdown — and his 49-yard contested catch in the third quarter set up James Cook's touchdown run before any of it. Moore did give the building one late scare, coming up limping after a fourth-down conversion and visiting the medical tent, but per NFL Network's Cameron Wolfe he said afterward that he was OK. Kincaid, questionable all week with a chest injury, caught four passes for 86 yards and the final touchdown. The record book will remember the quarterback. The film remembers that his two most-doubted pass catchers were the ones standing in the end zone.

The defense made sure the milestone came with a statement attached. A unit that allowed 28.5 points per game through its first six games, per the facts tracked all season from Athlon and AP reporting, held Baltimore to 144 total yards, forced three turnovers, and finished with four sacks and 12 quarterback hits, per Buffalowdown's recap of the win. Derrick Henry — the week-long subject of this site's Film Room — managed 53 yards on 11 carries. Honesty requires the context: Lamar Jackson injured his right thumb on Baltimore's first offensive snap when his throwing hand struck Greg Rousseau, per the Democrat and Chronicle's game coverage, and Ravens head coach Jesse Minter said Jackson needs thumb surgery and will be placed on injured reserve, per Reuters. Backup Tyler Huntley also left with a toe injury, and undrafted rookie Joe Fagnano finished his NFL debut 10 of 21 for 91 yards with an interception and a lost fumble. Even with all of that said on the record, head coach Joe Brady was not interested in discounts on Monday. Per NBC Sports, Brady said Sunday's defensive standard — the style, the communication, the way they flew around — is, in his words, what the expectation is now.

Even Saturday's emergency plan got its moment. This site wrote on game day about Buffalo signing Te'Cory Couch and elevating Geno Stone and A.J. Woods because the secondary was thin. Stone, elevated for the first time this season, tied for the team lead with six tackles, per Heavy's postgame reporting — and afterward sent the front office the shortest scouting report of the season: “Hey, I'm here.” On a weekend built around one franchise legend watching another, a practice-squad safety saying 'I'm here' and then proving it is about as Buffalo as a subplot gets.

But the image that will outlive the box score is the one in the stands. Kelly attended with his wife, Jill, per multiple reports of the milestone, and Jill Kelly shared her reaction to the record falling in one word, shared from the stadium: “Bittersweet.” Every Bills fan of a certain age understands that word in their bones. My first Bills game was Jim Kelly's last playoff game — a loss to Jacksonville, as my own Bills obsession was just getting started. There is a whole generation of us who learned this team through No. 12, through the K-Gun, through four Super Bowl runs that taught Buffalo how to hurt and hope in the same breath. Watching No. 17 pass him is not an erasure. It is the thing you prayed for during the 17-year playoff drought: that someday, somebody would be good enough to stand where Kelly stood and then reach one rung higher — and that Kelly would be there, healthy and home, to see it.

So where does it go from here? Buffalo is 6-1, winners of three straight, and heads to Minnesota for Monday Night Football on Nov. 9. The regular-season record — Kelly's 237 against Allen's 231 — is now a live countdown that could resolve itself before the snow does. Nobody passed a torch on Sunday with a speech or a ceremony. It happened on third-and-8, with 12:18 on the clock, in front of the man who set the standard and a stadium full of people who grew up on him. The record book has a new first line this morning. The standard it has to live up to is still wearing No. 12. Go Bills.

body: Teams tell you what they are worried about by what they do on Saturday. On Saturday — Halloween, no less — the Buffalo Bills signed defensive back Te'Cory Couch to the active roster and elevated safety Geno Stone and cornerback A.J. Woods from the practice squad, according to the Bills' PR announcement. Three defensive backs, added in three different ways, the day before the Baltimore Ravens and a returning Lamar Jackson arrive at Highmark Stadium for a 1 PM ET kickoff on CBS. That is not front-office housekeeping. That is a coaching staff looking at its secondary board, looking at Sunday's quarterback, and deciding it needed every available body.

Start with why the room was thin in the first place. Buffalo plays today without C.J. Gardner-Johnson, whose one-game suspension was upheld on appeal — he is out for the Ravens game and eligible to return Nov. 2. Next to that absence sits the week's quiet downgrade: slot corner Dee Alford, questionable on Friday's final report after going limited Wednesday and then not practicing Thursday or Friday with an ankle injury. Sports Illustrated reported Alford will likely be unavailable today, and that veteran Damar Hamlin will start in Gardner-Johnson's place. Add it up and Jim Leonhard's back end was down a suspended starter and trending down a nickel corner before Baltimore's team plane even landed.

So look at who Buffalo called. Stone is the headline of the three, and not just because of the position he plays. Per the reporting on Saturday's moves, Stone is expected to help cover Gardner-Johnson's absence — and he comes with a rare kind of scouting report: he played for the Ravens from 2020 to 2023 before spending the past two seasons with Cincinnati. There is no pretending a practice-squad elevation fixes a secondary by himself. But a safety who has sat in Baltimore's meeting rooms, elevated specifically for the week Baltimore comes to town, is the kind of detail that matters on third down. Couch and Woods, meanwhile, give Leonhard nickel and dime flexibility if Alford cannot go — options, plural, instead of one emergency plan.

They will need them, because the test is the real one. Jackson was a full participant all three days this week, carries no game designation, and Baltimore head coach Jesse Minter announced Friday that he will play after missing three straight games with a high ankle sprain. Jackson said Friday he is excited to be back on the field with his teammates and wants to put the Ravens in the win column. Yesterday's Film Room piece on this site broke down the choice that creates — Derrick Henry downhill or Zay Flowers in space — and nothing about Saturday's moves changes the math. What the moves change is how many different answers Buffalo can line up behind that choice, snap after snap, for four quarters.

The last word on who actually plays arrives at about 11:30 AM ET with the inactives, and Buffalo's list runs deeper than the secondary. Six Bills carried questionable tags on Friday's final report: right tackle Spencer Brown (back), wide receiver DJ Moore (shoulder), tight end Dalton Kincaid (chest), Alford, defensive lineman Greg Gaines (calf) and outside linebacker TJ Parker (knee, per the written official table). There is optimism mixed in — Kincaid told ESPN's Jeremy Fowler he was 'pretty confident' he would be able to play, per the Democrat and Chronicle, and Friday reporting had Moore expected to play barring a pregame setback — but optimism is not an inactive list, and this desk will not print it as one.

What Buffalo does not have to wonder about is its front. Ed Oliver, back after missing two games with a knee injury, and Bradley Chubb both finished the week as full participants with no designation, per Friday's report — the middle of this defense is as whole as it has been in a month. And the setting favors the home team: Buffalo is 5-1, off its bye, averaging an NFL-best 32.8 points per game, and, per Sports Illustrated, the Bills have won their last 11 games coming off a bye — a streak all eight experts on SI's prediction panel picked to reach 12 today against a 4-3 Ravens team that has lost two straight.

None of that plays a snap in the secondary, and that is the point. Buffalo spent its Saturday making sure a suspended starter and a wobbling ankle did not turn into a Sunday emergency against the most dangerous returning quarterback in football. Couch is signed, Stone and Woods are up, Hamlin steps in, and at 11:30 the inactives will finish the sentence. Then, at 1 PM, we find out whether three Halloween roster moves were just insurance — or the quiet reason Buffalo is 6-1 by dinner. Go Bills.

body: Here is the choice Jim Leonhard has to make before Sunday, and there is no version of it that takes everything away. The Baltimore Ravens come to Highmark Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 1 PM ET with Lamar Jackson back — a full participant all three days this week, no game designation on Friday's final report, and, per baltimoreravens.com, head coach Jesse Minter announced Friday that Jackson will play after missing three straight games with a high ankle sprain. With Jackson back, Baltimore gets its two-man stress test back with him: Derrick Henry downhill, and Zay Flowers everywhere else. As Athlon reported Saturday morning, Locked On Bills host Joe Marino put the dilemma plainly: Buffalo does not have to erase every Ravens weapon, but it cannot let Henry and Flowers control the game together. Film Room agrees — and the tape shows why letting both eat is how this game gets away.

Start with Henry, because he sets the math. In eight career meetings with Buffalo, Henry has averaged 102 rushing yards per game and scored 11 touchdowns — the history this site broke down earlier this week. The recent form is colder: 103 rushing yards total over his last two games at 3.02 yards a carry, a season average under 4.0 yards a carry for the first time in his career, and three straight games without a rushing touchdown. That slump is exactly why the tempting plan is to load the box, dare a returning quarterback to beat you, and finish the Henry argument early. It is also exactly the plan Baltimore wants you to declare — because every extra defender you walk down toward Henry is one less body where Flowers lives.

Flowers is not a complementary piece you clean up after the run is stopped. He is a screen, a jet motion, and a separation problem in one player. Against Cincinnati last week, per NBC Sports, Flowers turned a third-and-9 screen into a 48-yard touchdown and finished with 8 catches for 137 yards and a touchdown. That play is the whole warning: you do not have to throw deep to Flowers to lose to him. You just have to be outnumbered at the catch point, with your second level turned toward Henry and Jackson, and let him run after the catch into space your box count created. If Buffalo sells out early, Flowers does not need ten targets. He needs three touches in space.

Now look at who Buffalo has to solve that with. Ed Oliver is the good news in the middle: after missing the past two games with a knee injury, Oliver was a full participant Friday and carries no designation, per Friday's final report, and Bradley Chubb is cleared the same way. That interior help matters against Henry, because it lets Leonhard win some early-down snaps without stealing a safety to do it. The back end is thinner. Buffalo plays Sunday without C.J. Gardner-Johnson, whose one-game suspension was upheld on appeal — he is out for the Ravens game and eligible to return Nov. 2. Slot corner Dee Alford, meanwhile, is questionable after going limited Wednesday and then not practicing Thursday or Friday with an ankle injury, per Friday's report. A defense that ranks 31st in yards allowed and 28th in scoring defense at 28.5 points per game allowed, per the facts tracked from Athlon and AP reporting, does not have spare coverage answers to waste.

So what does the smart version look like on film? It is not a base defense. It is a series of early-down lies. Show Henry a loaded front before the snap, then rotate out of it after the handoff fake is sorted — make Baltimore declare run or pass before Buffalo declares its numbers. Keep two-high structure on the snaps Jackson is most likely to throw, bracket Flowers with leverage that pushes him back inside toward help, and accept that Mark Andrews and Rashod Bateman will get their underneath looks. That last part is the discipline Marino flagged, per Athlon: the complementary options cannot be allowed to become the reason Buffalo abandons its focus on the two primary threats. Four catches for Andrews hurt. Four explosive touches split between Henry and Flowers lose the game.

The other half of the pick-your-poison game is Buffalo's offense keeping Leonhard off the impossible snaps. Buffalo enters 5-1 to Baltimore's 4-3, at home and off the bye, with an offense Ravens Wire noted is averaging an NFL-best 32.8 points per game, and with James Cook averaging 5.34 yards per carry as the early-down engine. Every long Cook-and-Josh Allen drive is a drive where Henry and Flowers are watching, the box-count argument resets, and Jackson has to chase the game instead of dictating it. The quickest way to lose the dilemma is to fall behind early and spend the afternoon choosing in obvious passing and running situations, where Baltimore already knows which poison you picked.

Sunday inactives, about 90 minutes before kickoff, will settle the last variables — Spencer Brown, DJ Moore and Dalton Kincaid are all questionable for Buffalo after limited weeks, with Moore and Kincaid in non-contact jerseys throughout the week per Friday reporting, and their availability changes how much Buffalo can score its way out of a defensive mistake. But the central choice is already set. Take Henry's early-down efficiency away without handing Flowers the space to turn screens into touchdowns. Do one of those things and Buffalo can win a hard, honest game. Do neither, and both men will tell you by the fourth quarter which poison you actually picked: both. Go Bills.

body: Thursday was supposed to be the day Buffalo's injury picture finally cleared up. Instead it split in two. Ed Oliver — out the past two games with a knee injury — was a full participant in Thursday's practice, per the Bills' Thursday report reported by Buffalo Rumblings, after being limited on Wednesday. That is the single best development of Ravens week. And on the same report, the two names Buffalo could least afford to lose ground did exactly that: right tackle Spencer Brown missed practice for a second straight day with a back injury, and slot corner Dee Alford was downgraded from limited on Wednesday to a non-participant on Thursday with an ankle injury. Final game designations arrive Friday, and inactives land Sunday before the 1 PM ET kickoff against Baltimore at Highmark Stadium — but Thursday just told us where Friday's drama lives.

Start with Oliver, because everything about defending Baltimore starts in the middle. Oliver has missed Buffalo's last two games, and his absence has been the quiet hole in a defense that ranks 31st in yards allowed. A limited Wednesday was a step. A full Thursday is a different sentence entirely — it is what a player on track to play looks like in a normal week. Nothing is official until Friday's designations and Sunday's inactives, and this desk will not upgrade a practice report into a guarantee. But a defensive tackle going limited-to-full in 24 hours, after two games out, is trending exactly the way Buffalo needed him to trend with Derrick Henry and a returning Lamar Jackson coming to town.

Now the other edge of the line. Brown's back injury dates to the Oct. 12 game against the Los Angeles Rams, when he left in the second quarter. He returned six days later and played every snap against Las Vegas — and explained this week, in the quote of the week, what that took: 'I took enough drugs to sedate a small elephant in LA,' Brown said Wednesday, per the Democrat and Chronicle's reporting. He has not practiced since the bye — did not practice Wednesday, did not practice Thursday. Brown has said he remains optimistic and that head coach Joe Brady trusts his read on his own body, per Bills Wire — veterans earn that kind of leeway, and a Friday return in any capacity would change this conversation fast. If he cannot go, backup Tylan Grable is the likely starter at right tackle, per Bills reporting syndicated by Yardbarker. Against Baltimore's front, that is not a footnote. That is the matchup.

Alford's downgrade might be the sneakiest problem on the report. His ankle injury is not new — he first suffered it Oct. 4 against New England and missed the Rams game — and he played 43 of 66 defensive snaps in the win over Las Vegas, per the Bills on SI reporting. Limited Wednesday, out Thursday is the pattern that suggests a setback in practice, and Buffalo's depth behind him is thin: backup nickel Jordan Hancock remains on injured reserve, per that same reporting. Layer that on top of a secondary already playing Sunday without C.J. Gardner-Johnson, whose one-game suspension was upheld on appeal — he is out for the Ravens game and eligible to return Nov. 2 — and Jim Leonhard's coverage plan gets very honest, very quickly, against Jackson and Baltimore's receivers.

The rest of Thursday's Bills report was steadier. Wide receiver DJ Moore was limited for a second straight day as he works back from his shoulder injury after missing the past two games — two straight days of practice is encouraging, but his status for Sunday remains unconfirmed until Friday's designations. Tight end Dalton Kincaid (chest) and outside linebacker Bradley Chubb (chest/thumb) were also limited Thursday, per the report. Running back Ray Davis did not practice Thursday due to illness. None of those names moved backward on Thursday. Brown and Alford did — and in a week this big, movement is the story.

Baltimore's Thursday report moved the other way, and honesty requires saying so. Lamar Jackson was a full participant Thursday for a second straight day — his first full practices since Oct. 2 after missing three straight games with a high ankle sprain, per the Ravens' reports. Linebacker Roquan Smith and safety Kyle Hamilton both returned to practice Thursday as limited participants after missing Wednesday, per Ravens reporting. Even rookie guard Vega Ioane was back as a limited participant Thursday, just four days after an MCL sprain that was initially expected to cost him time. Baltimore is getting healthier on schedule. Buffalo is getting healthier in the middle — and thinner on the edges.

So Friday is the day. The final practice, the official questionable / doubtful / out designations, and the last real information before Sunday's inactives at Highmark. If Brown gets on the field Friday in any capacity and Alford returns, Thursday becomes a scare, not a verdict. If they miss a third day, Buffalo spends the weekend building contingency plans at right tackle and nickel corner for the biggest home game of the season so far. Oliver going full says the heart of this defense is coming back. Brown and Alford say the edges still have to be earned. Check back here Friday afternoon when the designations drop — that report, not this one, writes Sunday's starting lineup. Go Bills.

body: There are tougher ways to earn a locker room's respect than playing playoff football on a torn ACL. There just aren't many. On Wednesday, Tyrell Shavers practiced with the Buffalo Bills for the first time since that injury, designated to return from injured reserve ahead of Sunday's home game against the Baltimore Ravens — Nov. 1, 1 PM ET at Highmark Stadium. Head coach Joe Brady announced the move, and just like that, the best story in the building this week wasn't about a quarterback duel or an injury report. It was about a receiver who refused to leave a playoff game his knee had already left.

Go back to last season's Wild Card round against the Jacksonville Jaguars. Shavers hurt his knee in that game — an ACL injury, the kind that ends seasons and rewrites careers. He did not come out. Per Bills Wire's reporting on his return this week, Shavers did not exit the Jaguars game when he got hurt. He played through a torn ACL in a win-or-go-home playoff game. Read that sentence again, slowly, the way his teammates clearly have. That is not toughness as a talking point. That is a player deciding, in real time, that his team needed the version of him that was still standing.

Shavers called the road back exactly what it was. 'A long road,' he said, via Bills Wire. 'You learn a lot about yourself.' And then Josh Allen said the part that tells you how this story landed inside the room: 'It's awesome. He's got one of the best stories out there,' Allen said. 'He's one of the best teammates I've ever had.' Quarterbacks hand out compliments every week in this league — it's part of the job. 'One of the best teammates I've ever had' is not part of the job. That's a franchise quarterback telling you, on the record, what a guy on the roster's edge means to the people who actually share a huddle with him.

Now the honest part, because the Culture Desk doesn't sell timelines as guarantees. Being designated to return opens a 21-day practice window — it does not confirm Shavers will be active against Baltimore, or any specific Sunday. Bills Wire was clear on that point, and so are we: whether he dresses this week is still to be seen. A receiver coming back from an ACL injury has to stack practices, take contact, and prove the knee trusts him before the team trusts the knee in a game. Wednesday was step one. It was a big step one, but it was step one.

Which is exactly why this story fits Buffalo the way it does. This fan base has a type, and it has never been the loudest name on the marquee. It's the player who earns everything the hard way, who treats a roster spot like something you defend every single day, who plays special teams snaps and January snaps with the same desperation. Shavers played through a torn ACL in a playoff game. You cannot manufacture that kind of credibility, and you cannot fake your way into Allen saying what Allen said. In a week dominated by who is limited, who is full, and who is trending, Shavers' return is the reminder that some players' value never showed up on a participation report in the first place.

There is a football layer, too, and it matters without overstating it. Buffalo's receiver room is working through a real week: DJ Moore was limited in Wednesday's practice in a non-contact jersey as he works back from his shoulder injury, per Wednesday's reports — his status for Sunday is unconfirmed. Depth that a quarterback trusts is never a luxury in November, and a receiver Allen calls one of his best teammates is, at minimum, a name defensive coordinators and special teams coaches have to account for again soon, even if 'soon' turns out to be a week or two past the Ravens.

So welcome back, Tyrell. Whether the comeback becomes official under the lights on Sunday or a little further down the road, Wednesday already said plenty: the long road led back to the practice field, the quarterback who runs this franchise lit up talking about it, and a fan base that adopts grinders like family has a new favorite story to tell. Some returns are injury news. This one is Buffalo news. Go Bills.

body: Welcome back to The Tailgate, where the grill is hot, the opinions are hotter, and the NFL trade deadline — November 10, write it down — has turned every Bills fan I know into an amateur general manager with a group chat and absolutely no access to the salary cap spreadsheet. Buffalo is 5-1. The secondary has allowed 29 or more points in five of six games. And so the wishlist season is officially open. Today we rank the names floating around Bills Mafia by the only metric that matters in late October: delusion. From 'actually, that could happen' to 'sir, that man already plays for somebody else.'

No. 5 on the delusion scale — basically sober: Amani Hooker. This is the fresh one, and it is suspiciously reasonable, which is why it feels wrong to type. Athlon reported Wednesday morning that Bleacher Report's Kristopher Knox put the Tennessee safety at No. 10 on his trade block big board, named Buffalo and Washington as the suitors, and projected the price at a 2027 fourth-round pick. A fourth! For a starting safety on a 1-6 Titans team that has every reason to answer the phone! The coverage numbers travel with him, too: quarterbacks have posted an 81.2 passer rating throwing at Hooker this season per Pro Football Reference, and PFF's version is even kinder at 70.1, 17th among safeties. A real need, a real seller, a real price a 5-1 team can pay without mortgaging January. Delusion level: so low I had to check I was still on the internet.

No. 4 — one beer in: Zack Baun. Locked On Bills host Joe Marino called the Eagles linebacker his favorite deadline idea, and the logic is genuinely good, which is exactly how delusion gets its foot in the door. Baun played for defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard at Wisconsin, so he'd arrive already speaking the defense's language — no Rosetta Stone, no three-week adjustment period. The problem is the other end of the phone. Philadelphia has to voluntarily trade Buffalo a 29-year-old starter in the middle of the season, and contenders generally do not run a charity drive for other contenders. Possible? Sure. Likely? That's the beer talking.

No. 3 — the group chat is cooking: Budda Baker. Heavy reported Tuesday that Bleacher Report's Alex Kay put Buffalo at the top of his list of teams that could make a 'shock' trade, and the shock target is Arizona's eight-time Pro Bowler and four-time All-Pro. Baker is a phenomenal football player. He is also, per that same reporting, playing on a three-year, $54 million extension he signed in December 2024, under contract through next season — while Buffalo's available cap space sits around $4.1 million. Four point one. The math on this one doesn't need a calculator; it needs an intervention. Baker on this defense would be incredible. So would a heated driveway. I am getting neither, and for the same reason.

No. 2 — full tailgate confidence: Maxx Crosby. Every deadline season, somebody in the lot explains that actually, the Bills should simply acquire one of the best defensive players alive, as if he's a folding table somebody left by the dumpster. The case writes itself — ESPN's metrics have Crosby 8th among qualified pass rushers in pass-rush win rate at 27 percent and 6th in run-stop win rate at 32 percent — and the cost writes itself right back: the kind of draft capital that makes a front office need to sit down. Buffalo being named a 'potential landing spot' is doing heroic work in that headline. A landing spot is also what my driveway is for airplanes.

No. 1 — maximum delusion, hall-of-fame delusion, frame-it delusion: DeForest Buckner. Bills fans spent the weekend talking themselves into the Colts defensive tackle as Ed Oliver insurance — and I get it, the fit was beautiful, right up until the part where it stopped being available. Buckner has already been traded. To the 49ers. Reported Tuesday. He is, at time of writing, a member of a different football team, which I would describe as a significant obstacle to acquiring him, second only to his $26.6 million cap hit, which was always a non-starter against Buffalo's $4.1 million anyway. Wishing for Buckner now isn't optimism. It's a tribute band. The man is gone, the dream is gone, and somewhere a 49ers fan is having the exact conversation we were having on Saturday, except his ends with a jersey order.

So here's the Tailgate's official advice for the next thirteen days. Dream in the Hooker tax bracket: a real starter, from a real seller, for a pick that won't haunt anybody's draft party. Let the Baker and Crosby talk keep the group chat warm — that's what it's for — and pour one out for the Buckner era, which lasted one glorious weekend and produced zero defensive tackles. The deadline is November 10. The Ravens are Sunday, 1 PM ET at Highmark, and if the secondary holds up against a returning Lamar Jackson, half this wishlist gets quieter by Monday. If it doesn't? Clear your schedules. The delusion rankings get a sequel, and nobody in this fan base has ever once responded to a problem with less delusion. Go Bills.

body: Start with the respect, because the numbers earned it. Derrick Henry has averaged 102 rushing yards with 11 touchdowns in eight career meetings against Buffalo. That is not a matchup, that is a recurring nightmare, and every Bills fan old enough to remember those games can see the stiff-arm coming in their sleep. If Sunday were decided by history, this article would be a warning. It isn't, and it isn't.

Reason one: this is the coldest Henry has ever arrived. Over his last two games he has totaled 103 rushing yards at 3.02 yards a carry — barely half his career-meeting average against Buffalo, in two full games combined. His season average has fallen under 4.0 yards a carry for the first time, and he has gone three straight games without a rushing touchdown. Kings do not go three weeks without finding the end zone. Something is off, and it is showing up in every box score.

Reason two: the engine next to him is running at half power. Be honest about the caveat — Henry's quiet stretch coincided with Lamar Jackson being out, and defenses that don't have to honor Lamar's legs can load up on Henry. But Lamar's expected return Sunday comes with his own description of himself as restricted, on an ankle that has cost him three straight games since October 4. A pocket version of Lamar does not restore the read-option math that made Henry unstoppable. Buffalo's defense gets to play Henry straighter than any defense could when both men were healthy.

Reason three: Buffalo's run defense gets this test at home, off a bye, with two weeks to self-scout exactly this. Jim Leonhard's unit has heard all week that it ranks near the bottom of the league in yards allowed. What the yardage ranking hides is that this defense is built to rally and tackle in layers over long drives — and a 3.02-yards-a-carry back is exactly the kind of offense that has to string twelve plays together without a mistake to score. That is the game Buffalo wants to play.

Now the honest part, because this desk doesn't do propaganda. Ed Oliver has missed the last two games with a knee injury and his return is still in doubt — if he can't go, the interior of Buffalo's line is exactly where a desperate Henry would test first. Wednesday's practice report is the tell for both Oliver and Lamar, and if both trend the wrong way for Buffalo, this article gets a lot less comfortable. Check back here when it drops.

But as the week opens, the verdict stands: the scariest name on Baltimore's roster is bringing his worst form of the season into the building where Buffalo plays its best football. The crown is heavy. Lately, it has also been slipping. NOT THE KING — not on Sunday.
