body: For ten years, the first name on Buffalo's scouting report when Baltimore — or Tennessee before them — came up on the schedule was the same one: Derrick Henry. And the numbers explain why nobody in Orchard Park ever talked themselves out of worrying about him. In eight career meetings with the Bills, Henry has averaged 102 rushing yards per game and scored 11 touchdowns. Not one good afternoon in there propping up the average. A decade of him, at full speed, being the worst Sunday on Buffalo's calendar.

Now open this season's book, because the King on those pages is somebody else. Over the last two weeks, Henry has rushed for 103 yards — total. Not per game. Total. In two games combined he barely matched what he used to take from Buffalo in one, and he did it at 3.02 yards per carry, a number that belongs to a short-yardage back getting stacked up at the line, not to the most feared power runner of his generation.

Zoom out and the season tells the same story. Henry is averaging 3.9 yards per carry this year. Read that again: for the first time in his 11-year career, Derrick Henry is under 4.0 yards a carry. Eleven seasons of defensive coordinators building entire game plans around keeping him at exactly that number, and this is the first year the number has just... shown up. On film, a sub-4.0 power back season has a look: first contact arriving a half-step sooner, the pile falling backward instead of forward, second-and-9 turning into third-and-long instead of third-and-manageable. The stiff-arm highlights are built on momentum. The momentum is what goes first.

Now the honest part, because Film Room doesn't bury a player on half the evidence. Henry hasn't scored a rushing touchdown in three straight games — and those are exactly, precisely, the three games Lamar Jackson has missed. That's not a coincidence to wave past; it's the context the whole league understands. Without Jackson's legs bending the defense, every safety, every linebacker, every spare set of eyes on the field belongs to Henry. Eleven men get to play one back honestly. His quiet stretch and Lamar's absence are the same three weeks, and any breakdown that ignores that is selling you a funeral the film doesn't support.

Which is what makes Sunday at Highmark — Ravens at Bills, 1 PM ET — the most interesting test of the season for Jim Leonhard's defense. Jackson is expected back. If he plays, Henry gets his shield back: a defense that has to honor the quarterback's legs can't sell out the same way. But the cliff numbers didn't need Lamar's absence to exist — the 3.9 season average was built over the whole year, not three weeks. So Sunday isn't really Henry versus Buffalo. It's two true stories colliding: a back whose decade of dominance is over on the numbers, and a back whose worst month came with an excuse Buffalo won't get to use.

Leonhard's answer, on paper, is the aggressive one: sell out on early downs. Load the box on first and second down, make Henry win against numbers — the thing this season says he no longer does — and dare Baltimore to live in third-and-long, where a returning quarterback has to drop back, set his feet, and throw on schedule. It's the plan everybody claims they'll run against Henry and nobody has survived running for ten years. The difference now is the arithmetic finally backs the coordinator up: at 3.02 a carry over the last two weeks, even an honest box is winning.

One wrinkle Buffalo has to solve without help: Ed Oliver's return is doubtful. Don't let anybody tell you he's back — as of this writing, the middle of Buffalo's defensive front probably has to hold up without its best interior disrupter, against the biggest back of the era, in a game plan built on winning at the line of scrimmage. That's the stress point. Leonhard's sell-out works only if the front wins its gaps without Oliver collapsing the interior by himself — numbers and discipline instead of a star.

Joe Brady's side of it matters too: every long Buffalo drive is a drive Henry watches from the sideline, and a rested defense is the one that tackles a 247-pound back in the fourth quarter. But the headline is the headline. For a decade, this matchup was simple: stop Henry or lose. On Sunday, for the first time in 11 years, the numbers say Henry has to prove he's still the problem. So here's my question for Bills Mafia: is this the week the King finally looks mortal in Buffalo — or does Lamar's return bring him back to life for one more Sunday?

body: The bye week is over, the Ravens are coming to Orchard Park on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 1 PM ET, and the only question that matters has followed Buffalo out of the bye: which version of Lamar Jackson shows up? The reports out of Baltimore this week have pointed toward Jackson returning to the lineup after missing time — and on paper, a two-time MVP coming back sounds like bad news for the home team. Dig one layer down, and it might be the best news the Bills got all week.

Here is what we actually know, versus what is being assumed. Jackson has missed Baltimore's recent games. He has said himself, earlier this month, that if he pushed it he would be restricted — his word was that he'd be "a statue" back there. That is not a beat writer's guess. That is the quarterback describing his own ankle. A Lamar Jackson who cannot threaten the edge is a completely different problem for a defense to solve, and defensive coordinator Jim Leonhard knows it.

Leonhard's unit has taken its lumps this season — the Bills sit 31st in yards allowed, a number you'll see in every preview this week. But yards were never the whole story with this group, and a pocket-bound Jackson plays directly into what Buffalo can still do: rush with discipline, keep everything in front, and make a limited quarterback win with methodical drives instead of explosives.

On the other side of the ball, the math is simpler. Buffalo comes in 5-1, rested, at home, with an offense built around balance. James Cook is averaging 5.34 yards per carry on 627 rushing yards — the engine that lets head coach Joe Brady control tempo and keep his own defense off the field. If Buffalo owns the clock, Baltimore's returning quarterback spends the afternoon watching, which is exactly where you want a guy shaking off rust.

None of this makes Sunday a lock, and anybody telling you otherwise is selling something. Jackson at 80 percent is still one of the most dangerous players alive, and the Ravens know their season tilts on this game. But the version of this matchup that terrified Bills fans in September — full-speed Lamar, full playbook, no restrictions — is not the version walking into Highmark on Sunday, at least not according to Lamar himself.

The official word comes with the inactives ninety minutes before kickoff. Until then, the smartest read is the one the quarterback gave us: he's coming back, and he's coming back restricted. For a 5-1 team coming off its bye, at home, with the AFC's top seed in reach — yes, that qualifies as great news.

We'll have the Film Room breakdown of how Leonhard should attack a limited Jackson later this week, the Culture Desk on what this game means in the building, and The Tailgate with the disrespect rankings on Friday. Ravens week is here. Go Bills.

articles.author: Matt Manzella
body: Every week, the national conversation about Buffalo starts and ends with Josh Allen. That's understandable — he's the franchise. But if you want to understand why this offense stays on schedule, why third downs stay manageable, and why Joe Brady can call a game without panic, start with a different number: 5.34. That's James Cook's yards-per-carry average this season, on 627 rushing yards, and it might be the most important stat on the team.

Start with what 5.34 does to a play sheet. A league-average first-down run leaves you second-and-six. Cook's average leaves Buffalo at second-and-five or better, and half the time it simply moves the chains or flips the field position battle entirely. When your early-down run game produces like that, the defensive coordinator across from you can never be right: stack the box and Allen beats you over the top; play coverage and Cook bleeds you four, six, nine yards at a time.

Watch the Ravens-week film from earlier this season and you'll see the pattern in his runs. Cook's gift isn't just speed — it's patience behind the zone scheme, one cut, and then vertical. He presses the hole long enough to move the second-level defender, and the moment that defender commits, the cut goes against his leverage. It's why so many of his carries that look like three-yard gains on contact turn into seven by the whistle.

The second layer is what Cook does to the passing game without touching the ball. Play-action only works when linebackers believe the run. With Cook averaging over five a carry, they have no choice — the first step is toward the line on nearly every fake, and that half-step is the window Allen throws into. Some of Buffalo's easiest completions this season start with a linebacker respecting Cook too much.

There's a workload point here too. 627 yards through six games is a real load, but Cook's efficiency means Buffalo isn't grinding him into dust to get production — he's not a 25-carry battering ram, he's a per-touch problem. Keeping him fresh into January is a quiet priority you can see in how Brady rotates the backfield on early downs.

Sunday against Baltimore, this is the matchup underneath the matchup. The Ravens will game-plan for Allen first — everybody does. If Cook gets his usual efficiency early, that plan collapses by the second quarter, and Buffalo controls the kind of game a 5-1 team should control at home.
The headline will say Allen versus Jackson. The film says the game tilts on whether Baltimore can make somebody other than No. 4 beat them — and right now, No. 4 is happily letting them try.

body: Good morning, Bills Country. The bye week is in the rearview, Buffalo sits at 5-1, and the Ravens come to Highmark Stadium on Sunday, Nov. 1 at 1 PM ET. Here's everything you need to start the week, in the order you'll argue about it.

THE LAMAR WATCH. All eyes are on Baltimore's quarterback situation. Reports this week have pointed toward Lamar Jackson returning after missing time — but Jackson himself said earlier this month that he'd be restricted, and the official answer doesn't arrive until Sunday's inactives. Our top story today breaks down why a limited Lamar might quietly be great news for Buffalo.

THE FILM ROOM IS OPEN. The Film Room leads with the number nobody's talking about: James Cook, 5.34 yards per carry, 627 rushing yards. If you read one thing before Sunday, make it that — it's the stat Baltimore's defense has to solve first, before it even gets to Josh Allen.

TRADE DEADLINE SEASON. The Nov. 10 deadline is two weeks out, and our five-part board series starts today with the secondary. Buffalo's cap room is tight — roughly $4.1 million by the numbers floating around the league — so this series is about fits, not fantasies. One name a day, starting this afternoon.

ON THE INJURY AND DISCIPLINE FRONT. The C.J. Gardner-Johnson suspension was upheld, so he's out for the Ravens game and eligible to return Nov. 2 — plan the secondary conversation accordingly. Sam Franklin Jr., meanwhile, won his appeal and is cleared for Nov. 1. Both facts matter for how Jim Leonhard builds Sunday's game plan, and both are now settled, which is more than we could say a week ago.

FROM THE CULTURE DESK. Our DJ Moore column lands today: a receiver who chose Buffalo, a fan base that adopts its players, and what has to happen off the field before the Moore era works on it. Moore's return from his shoulder sprain is still an "expected back" situation rather than a confirmed one — watch the practice reports Wednesday through Friday before you lock in your expectations either way.

AND FINALLY, THE FUN STUFF. The Tailgate's weekly disrespect rankings are live, and this week's No. 1 will start arguments. Friday brings our Ravens open thread and score-prediction poll. body: Here is the riddle of the 2026 Bills: the defense ranks 31st in yards allowed, and the team is 5-1. Both things are true, both things matter, and the space between them is where Jim Leonhard's defense actually lives. If you only read the yardage ranking, you'd conclude this unit is a disaster propped up by Josh Allen. The film tells a more uncomfortable story — for opponents.

Start with the philosophy. Leonhard's defense is built to defend space in layers, not to win every snap. The structure concedes the cheap stuff — the six-yard completion, the four-yard run — in exchange for taking away the explosive play that flips a game in one snap. Offenses can absolutely drive on this defense. What they find, over and over, is that driving 80 yards without a mistake is a different skill than driving 40.

That's the math people miss. Every additional play in a drive is another chance for a penalty, a drop, a tipped ball, a protection bust. Long drives against this defense die of a thousand cuts more often than they end in touchdowns, and the scoreboard — the only stat that has Buffalo at 5-1 — reflects it. Yards are a volume stat. Points are a verdict. This defense keeps winning the verdict.

The second piece is situational. Watch what happens when the field shrinks. In open field, Buffalo's coverage can look soft, almost indifferent. Inside the opponent's final 30 yards, the picture changes: the windows close faster, the rush gets home quicker, and the margin for an offense's error disappears. A defense that looks the same everywhere is a defense that can be solved. This one changes its personality when the game gets expensive.

Now the honest part, because Film Room doesn't do propaganda: there is usually one drive per game where the structure genuinely wobbles. A miscommunication, a substitution caught late, a series where the rush and the coverage aren't married up — and suddenly an offense is walking down the field like the first three quarters were a rumor. Against playoff-caliber quarterbacks, that one drive is the season. It's the thing that has to get fixed, and the bye week was the time to fix it.

Sunday's test is a strange one: a Baltimore offense whose quarterback is expected back but has described himself as restricted. A limited Lamar Jackson tests exactly what this defense is built to do — rally, tackle, and make an offense earn every yard over twelve plays instead of two.

So no, the 31st ranking isn't fake, and it isn't the whole truth either. This defense gives up yards by design and Sundays by accident. Six games in, the design is winning. January will grade the final exam.

articles.author: Matt Manzella
body: Let's start with something that doesn't happen by accident: DJ Moore is a Buffalo Bill because Buffalo went and got him from Chicago, yes — but players of his caliber have a say in where they land in this league, and Moore landed here with his eyes open. He picked the cold. He picked the smallest market in the conference. He picked us. The Culture Desk has one request: let's act like it.

Buffalo does something no other fan base in football does quite the same way. We adopt. A player shows up, works, respects the city, and within a season he's family — his charity gets flooded, his restaurant order becomes local news, his kids could run for mayor. It's the best recruiting pitch this franchise owns, better than any facility tour: come here and be loved like a son, as long as you give us everything on Sunday.

But adoption has a flip side, and this is where we have to be honest with ourselves. The same passion that lifts players up can turn a slow start into a verdict. Moore is coming back from a shoulder sprain — his return has been "expected" since before the bye, not confirmed — and a receiver's timing with a quarterback is built in weeks, not in one Sunday. If the first two games back are quiet, that is not a referendum on the trade. That is a guy learning where Josh Allen wants him at the top of a route while 70,000 of us hold our breath.

Here's what the Moore era needs off the field first: patience with a purpose. This offense doesn't need him to be a hero in November. It needs him to be the player defenses have to account for in January — the one who makes a coordinator choose between Cook, the tight ends, and a receiver who can take a slant to the house. That version of Moore arrives on a curve, not on a deadline.

There's a locker-room layer too. Moore walks into a room with an established hierarchy and a quarterback who is the sun everything orbits. The receivers who have thrived here are the ones who understood that early and made themselves essential inside it. Everything in Moore's career says he's a worker, not a diva. Trust the worker.

So here's the deal, Buffalo. He picked us — the city, the weather, the whole beautiful frozen package. Let's return the favor the Buffalo way: loud, patient, and all in. When No. 2 breaks his first big one at Highmark, the sound is going to tell him everything about where he landed.
Welcome home, DJ. Now let's go get you a January to remember.

body: The NFL trade deadline hits Nov. 10, and for the next five weekdays this series will put one name on the board per day — a real fit, a real price, and a real verdict. Today is the overview, and it starts with the position everybody in Buffalo is already looking at: the secondary.

The need is not subtle. C.J. Gardner-Johnson's suspension was upheld, which puts him out for the Ravens game on Nov. 1 and eligible to return Nov. 2 — a short absence, but a revealing one, because it showed how thin the margin is behind the starters. Christian Benford has had a harder season than his reputation suggests. Tre'Davious White is on the practice squad. You don't need a film degree to see where the front office is shopping.

Now the constraint that runs this whole series: money. Buffalo's available cap space sits around $4.1 million, which means every name on this board has to survive two tests — the acquisition cost in draft capital, and the contract cost in real cap room. The fantasy trades filling your timeline fail at least one of those tests. The five names in this series pass both, at least on paper.

The names analysts have linked to Buffalo's situation tell you the shape of the market: veteran safety help like Arizona's Budda Baker at the expensive end, younger options like the Jets' Andre Cisco in the middle, and a corner like Philadelphia's Riq Woolen as the swing-for-upside play. Whether any of those specific players move is a different question — this week we'll work through the secondary option first, then the rest of the board, one honest evaluation at a time.

Two ground rules for the series. First, no name appears here without a plausible cap path — if the money doesn't work, we'll say so and move on. Second, standing pat is a legitimate outcome. A 5-1 team with a defense ranked 31st in yards sounds like a buyer, and it probably is, but a bad trade is worse than no trade, and Buffalo's recent history says this front office would rather overpay in April than in November.

There's also a wide receiver wrinkle we'll get to mid-series: Joshua Palmer's name has surfaced in trade-candidate chatter from the other direction — as a player Buffalo could move. That's a harder conversation than the secondary shopping, and it deserves its own day.

The board starts tomorrow with the secondary target who fits best. Five days, five names, no fantasy football. If Buffalo does nothing by Nov. 10, you'll at least know exactly what nothing cost — and what it saved.

body: If you only watch highlights, Keon Coleman's season looks like a rumor — a catch here, a touchdown there, long stretches where the broadcast forgets him. Then you open the actual numbers and the story flips: 19 catches, 283 yards, 3 touchdowns, and the two figures that should end the argument about whether he's arrived. Zero drops. And a 138.0 passer rating when Josh Allen throws his way.

Let's sit with the zero for a second. Drops were the cloud over Coleman's early career — the plays that reached his hands and didn't stay there, the drives that died on contact. This season: 19 catches on a 79.2 percent catch rate, and not one drop. That isn't luck. That's a receiver whose hands have caught up to his frame, securing the ball through contact instead of fighting it. The most important development in a young receiver's game is never the spectacular play. It's the ordinary play becoming automatic.

283 yards on 19 catches works out to nearly 15 yards a reception, which tells you how Buffalo is using him: not as a volume target, but as a strike weapon. Coleman isn't catching five-yard hitches to move the chains. He's winning downfield, at the catch point, in the areas where a 50-50 ball becomes a 70-30 ball because of his size and timing. Three touchdowns, in three straight games at one stretch, is what that usage looks like when it cashes.

The 138.0 rating when targeted deserves context too. That number measures what happens when Allen decides Coleman is the answer on a given play — completions, yards, touchdowns, and the absence of interceptions. A rating that high means Allen's trust isn't charity. The quarterback who can throw to anybody is choosing Coleman in real moments, and the results keep justifying it.

On film, you can see why. Coleman has become precise in the places young receivers are usually sloppy: stemming his routes to hold a defender's leverage, sitting down in the zone void instead of drifting into coverage, and — this is the quiet one — blocking with genuine intent in the run game. In an offense where James Cook averages 5.34 yards a carry, a receiver who blocks like he means it isn't a bonus. He's part of the machinery.

So why does the breakout feel quiet? Because Buffalo's offense spreads the ball by design, and because Coleman doesn't chase the spotlight the way the position's divas do. The stat line isn't lying about his talent. It's lying about his role — making a foundational piece look like a role player, one efficient Sunday at a time.

With DJ Moore working back and the Ravens' secondary on deck, Coleman's next step is volume when the defense tilts away from him. The efficiency is already there. When the targets climb to match it, the highlights will finally catch up to the numbers.

body: Welcome back to the only power rankings with the courage to rank on vibes, grudges, and whatever happened most recently. The Bills are 5-1 and spent the bye resting, which gave me seven days to watch the rest of the AFC and take detailed notes on why each of them should be disrespected. Let's begin.

No. 5: The Baltimore Ravens (disrespect level: respectful, unfortunately). You're next on the schedule, your quarterback has spent the week as a league-wide injury mystery, and your season is somehow both alive and on life support. I would love to rank you higher on this list, but it's hard to disrespect a team whose entire fan base is currently refreshing injury reports like it's election night. See you Sunday. Bring the statue.

No. 4: The New England Patriots (disrespect level: nostalgic). Every few years, Patriots fans convince themselves the empire is back because they beat a team with a losing record in October. It's adorable — a retired magician doing card tricks at a children's party and insisting he could still headline Vegas. Sir, we remember. We also remember the last five years. Sit down.

No. 3: The Miami Dolphins (disrespect level: meteorological). The Dolphins are a September team the way a convertible is a January car in Buffalo — technically legal, spiritually unserious. Every year it's the same documentary: fastest show on turf until the temperature drops below 50, at which point the entire offense files a weather complaint. Your stadium has a beach club. Our stadium has a parking lot where a man grills in a blizzard for fun. We are not the same.

No. 2: The New York Jets (disrespect level: structural). The Jets are a group project where nobody did the reading, the presentation is tomorrow, and somehow the loudest guy in the group still thinks it's going great. Decades of drafts, free-agent splashes, prime-time hype — and the most consistent thing about the Jets is the camera finding a fan doing the math on when pitchers and catchers report. I don't even dislike the Jets anymore. I study them, the way scientists study a frog that keeps jumping into the same pond.

No. 1: The Kansas City Chiefs (disrespect level: maximum, permanent, non-negotiable). The Chiefs are simultaneously washed, inevitable, lucky, doomed, and somehow already in the AFC Championship Game in everyone's bracket. Their fans have reached the stage of dynasty where a regular-season win gets a shrug and a regular-season loss gets a congressional inquiry. I disrespect them because they are the mountain, and because somebody in this conference has to say it out loud every week until somebody knocks them off it. Preferably in January. Preferably here.

That's the list. The Bills return from the bye on Sunday against Baltimore, 1 PM ET at Highmark, and a win moves the disrespect index in a healthier direction: outward, at everyone else, where it belongs. Disagree with the rankings? The comments are open, and so is my group chat. Choose wisely.

body: This article is a paid promotion. Sunday, Nov. 1 at 1 PM ET, the Ravens come to Highmark Stadium, the Bills come off their bye at 5-1, and if you're reading this without a ticket in hand, you are officially in the part of the week where a plan beats a panic. Here's the game plan.

First, the market reality. A 5-1 home team, a marquee opponent, and a fan base that treats late-October football like a religious obligation means prices on the secondary market move with the news cycle. Lamar Jackson's status is the single biggest price lever of the week: clarity about Baltimore's quarterback — either way — tends to firm prices up, so the cheapest window of the week is usually during the uncertainty, not after it resolves. If you have a price you're comfortable with, don't get cute waiting for a collapse that a national TV slot rarely delivers.

Second, where to sit. For a first game, the lower bowl between the 20s is the dream and prices like it. The value sweet spot for most fans is the upper deck's first several rows — you get the full-field view that actually teaches you the game, the crowd energy is unmatched, and your wallet survives the trip. End zone seats are the loudest ride in the building; just know the play moves away from you for a quarter at a time. And wherever you sit, check the listing for aisle and row details before you buy — in a sold-out building, two seats can share a section and not share an experience.

Third, buy verified. Use a marketplace that guarantees your ticket and your entry — price-shopping across the screenshot economy is how Sundays get ruined in the parking lot. Compare the all-in price, fees included, not the headline number, and screenshot your confirmation before you leave the house. If you're buying for a group, one person buys all the seats in a single order; split orders are how best friends end up in different time zones of the stadium.

Fourth, think past this Sunday. The new stadium era is reshaping what a Bills ticket means — demand is only moving one direction, and the fans who build a routine now (verified accounts ready, price alerts set, group chat organized) are the ones who never miss a game they wanted to see. Treat Ravens week like a rehearsal for January, because if this team does what we think it's about to do, January is coming to Orchard Park.

However you get in — lower bowl, upper deck, or the last row under the lights — get in. A 5-1 team, a returning MVP storyline, and a Sunday afternoon at Highmark is the good stuff. We'll see you there. Go Bills.
